Z0.p: A general heading for formulaic devices in storytelling: set phrases and repeated patterns that shape how a tale is told.

Z10.r: *Hdwb. d. Märchens s.v. “Formel”; Irish myth: *Cross; India: *Thompson-Balys.
Z10.p: Standard opening, closing, and linking phrases that frame a tale from start to finish.

Z10.1.r: *Hdwb. d. Märchens II 161; *BP IV 14ff.; Korean: Zong in-Sob 14 No. 7.
Z10.1.p: Set phrases used to open a tale.

Z10.2.r: *BP IV 24ff.; Hdwb. d. Märchens II 164; *Petsch Formelhafte Schlüsse im Volksmärchen (1900); India: *Thompson-Balys.
Z10.2.p: Set phrases used to close a tale.

Z10.3.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens II 162; BP IV 20ff.
Z10.3.p: Set phrases used to move the story from one part to the next.

Z11.r: *Type 2300; *BP II 209; Taylor Hdwb. d. Märchens II 190a; Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
Z11.p: A tale worded so it can go on indefinitely, such as hundreds of sheep carried over a stream one at a time.

Z11.1.p: An endless tale in which corn is carried away one grain at a time.

Z11.2.p: An endless tale in which hundreds of birds caught in a snare fly away one at a time.

Z12.r: “If the bowl had been stronger my tale had been longer.” *Types 2250, 2260; BP II 210, III 455; Taylor Hdwb. d. Märchens II 189b; Köhler-Bolte I 269.
Z12.p: A tale that breaks off just as it gets interesting, because the narrator stops. It is a joking ending used as a formula.

Z13.r: Type 2200; England, U.S., Canada: *Baughman; West Indies: Flowers 586.
Z13.p: A catch tale: its telling forces the listener to ask a particular question, and the teller gives a ridiculous answer.

Z13.1.p: A catch tale in which the teller frightens the listener by shouting "Boo" at the exciting point.

Z13.2.p: A catch tale in which the teller is killed within his own story.

Z14.p: Set, stock passages within a tale, usually recited in a different voice from the rest of the narration.

Z15.p: A tale told without using any pronouns such as he, she, or it.

Z16.r: *Type 653; *BP III 45; Basset RTP VII 188; Cosquin Revue d’Ethnographie et des Traditions Populaires I 62, II 41; Africa: Werner African 359.
Z16.p: A tale that ends with a question put to the listener.

Z16.1.p: A tale ending with a question, in which four brothers construct a woman.

Z17.r: Type 2350; Taylor JAFL XLVI 88, Hdwb. d. Märchens II 190; U.S.: Baughman; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2300; India: Thompson-Balys.
Z17.p: Stories that begin over and over again and repeat, so the tale keeps restarting from its opening lines.

Z18.p: Stock conversations that recur in folk tales as a fixed formula, with set questions and answers repeated word for word.

Z18.1.p: A stock exchange in which a character asks why another has such big ears, and is told they are for hearing better. This is the formula from the tale of the wolf disguised as a grandmother.

Z19.p: Miscellaneous framework devices in which a tale is built around a set structure or pattern not covered by the other formula groups.

Z19.1.p: Tales built around a game, in which the story is told as a game or played out through its rules.

Z19.2.p: Tales deliberately full of contradictions, where statements and events cancel each other out.

Z20.r: (Kettenmärchen.) **Taylor JAFL XLVI 77ff.; *Types 2000—2199; Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish American: Boas JAFL XXV 219ff., 292f., Espinosa JAFL XXVII 222ff.; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 316; cf. Nouvelles de Sens No. 31.
Z20.p: Cumulative tales, where a story is built as a chain of links, each new event added to all the earlier ones and repeated in order.

Z20.1.p: Cumulative tales that are pure nonsense, with a chain of absurd links that have no logical sense.

Z21.p: Chain tales built on counting, where each link follows a numerical sequence such as doubling or counting upward.

Z21.1.r: **Taylor JAFL XLVI 79 No. 2009; *Livingston MLN XLV 246—51; Murray History of Chess (Oxford, 1913) 207—9, 755; India: Thompson-Balys.
Z21.1.p: The tale explaining how chess was invented. The inventor asks for one grain of wheat on the first square of the board, two on the second, four on the third, doubling each time, and the king cannot pay the reward.

Z21.1.1.p: A version of the chess reward tale in which a master pays wages by doubling a grain of rice each harvest, and in the end has no fields left to give.

Z22.r: **Espinosa Revista de Filologia Española XVII 390ff.; *Taylor JAFL XLVI 79 No. 2010; *Greenleaf Ballads and Sea-songs of Newfoundland (Cambridge, Mass., 1933) 93 No. 41; **Hdwb. d. Märchens II 171ff.; *Newell “The Carol of the Twelve Numbers” JAFL IV (1891) 215—220; Köhler-Bolte III 370 n. 2; BP III 15 n.—Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2010*; Russian: Andrejev No. 812B*; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 156 No. 2045*; Jewish: *Neuman.
Z22.p: Chain tales in which the numbers one to twelve are each linked to a set of objects, often with religious meaning, and the list is recited cumulatively.

Z22.1.r: **Taylor JAFL XLVI 79 No. 2010A, Hdwb. d. Märchens II 172b; Kristensen Danske Dyrefabler 146—60 Nos. 337—348; Fb “Juledagsgave” I 54, IV 248; T. Norlind Svenska Allmogens Liv@2 612.
Z22.1.p: The cumulative Christmas song counting the twelve gifts of Christmas, from one partridge up to twelve lords, each day adding a new gift.

Z22.2.r: **Taylor JAFL XLVI 80 No. 2010B, Hdwb. d. Märchens II 172b; Kristensen Danske Dyrefabler 150—54 Nos. 351—370.
Z22.2.p: A cumulative counting list pairing each number from one to twelve with a kind of food, from partridge up to cheeses.

Z23.r: **Taylor JAFL XLVI 80 No. 2010 I; Kristensen Danske Dyrefabler 168—78 Nos. 392—418; *T. Norlind Svenska Allmogens Liv@2 (Stockholm, 1925) 612. — Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2010 I*.
Z23.p: A farmer pays his servant each year with an animal or thing, adding to the earlier payments, from a hen up to a girl and a farmstead.

Z24.r: (First ed. Z21.4.) He thus discovers that it is Sunday. *Taylor JAFL XLVI 80 No. 2012, Hdwb. d. Märchens II 174b.
Z24.p: A forgetful man who cannot recall the days of the week runs through them one by one, with an event for each day.

Z24.1.p: A widower recounts his courtship, marriage, and his wife's death all within a single week, packing a whole life into the days.

Z24.1.1.r: at ten my child’s soul was crowned in heaven.” *Taylor JAFL XLVI 80 No. 2012B.
Z24.1.1.p: A life story told in ten hours, beginning with the speaker's birth at one o'clock and moving through the hours of his life.

Z24.1.2.r: in August I have nothing more to do with my young.” *Taylor JAFL XLVI 80 No. 2012C.
Z24.1.2.p: A bird advises a man to treat his lazy children as she treats her young, with the bird describing how she builds her nest from March onward.

Z24.1.3.r: *Taylor JAFL XLVI 80 No. 2012D; Halliwell Nursery Rhymes of England 33 No. 49.
Z24.1.3.p: The nursery rhyme Solomon Grundy, which tells a whole life in days, from being born on Monday to being buried on Sunday.

Z25.p: A fly cannot remember her own name and goes around asking a series of creatures and objects, such as a woodcutter, an axe, and a tree, but none can tell her. At last a foal inside a mare's belly says her name is "fly."

Z30.p: A category for cumulative chain tales in which the links all happen within one scene or event, and the characters do not depend on one another's actions.

Z31.r: Taylor JAFL XLVI 81 Nos. 2019—2020; Hdwb. d. Märchens II 176a.
Z31.p: A cumulative chain tale built around a wedding, where the chain of characters or actions takes place at the wedding.

Z31.1.r: *Type 2019; *BP III 71; *Taylor JAFL XLVI 81 No. 2019; India: Thompson-Balys.
Z31.1.p: A wedding chain tale in which a suitor is sent from one relative to another to ask each for permission to marry.

Z31.2.p: A louse and a flea want to marry, and a series of small creatures such as mosquito, toad, and ant offer to supply the wedding feast.

Z32.p: A cumulative chain tale about a death, where the chain consists of animal characters reacting to the death in a series.

Z32.1.r: *Type 2021; *BP II 147 n. 1; *Wesselski Hessische Blätter f. Vksk. XXXII 2ff.; *Taylor JAFL XLVI 82 No. 2021.
Z32.1.p: A funeral procession for a hen in which animals join one by one. The funeral carriage breaks down or the procession ends in drowning.

Z32.1.1.r: *Taylor JAFL XLVI 82 No. 2021A; BP II 146; **Haavio FFC XCIX; **Wesselski Hessische Blätter f. Vksk. XXXII 2ff.
Z32.1.1.p: A cock chokes to death and the hen goes asking for help from a series of things and people, such as a stream, a tree, a pig, a miller, and a baker, none of whom will act.

Z32.2.r: (First ed. Z31.2.2.) *Taylor JAFL XLVI 82 No. 2022A; *BP I 293; Parsons JAFL XXXIII 37; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys.
Z32.2.p: A cumulative tale in which a little hen dies and is mourned by a series of animals and objects, each of which is in turn mourned by others in a chain.

Z32.2.1.r: Each act of mourning described by a neologism: the table untables itself. (First ed. Z31.2.2.1.) (Cf. X1506.) *Taylor JAFL XLVI 82 No. 2022A, Hdwb. d. Märchens II 177a; Tegethoff Französische Märchen II 78 No. 18; Rolland Rimes et jeux d’enfance (1881) 119f.; Kristensen Danske Dyrefabler 98ff. No. 171ff.
Z32.2.1.p: The death of the little hen is told using unusual or elaborate wording, as a stylistic feature of the tale.

Z32.3.r: (First ed. Z31.2.3.) *Taylor FFC XLVI 82 No. 2023; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 154 No. 2023*; Italian: Crane Italian Popular Tales (1885) 376—77.
Z32.3.p: A little ant finds a penny, buys new clothes, and sits in her doorway. Animals propose marriage, but she rejects those whose sounds she dislikes and marries a quiet mouse, who then drowns in the stew. In grief, various birds and animals mutilate themselves.

Z32.4.p: A master orders his servant to kill the hen, and she begs to be spared. He then sends the servant after a series of other animals, such as a rooster, goose, rabbit, toad, and tiger, in turn.

Z32.5.r: “But who is Tulsi Das?” The report is traced back to the washerman, who says: “He was my ass.” India: *Thompson-Balys.
Z32.5.p: A mourning chain about a dead donkey, in which the mourning passes from a washerman up to the queen.

Z33.r: (Members of the chain not interrelated.) Taylor JAFL XLVI 83 Nos. 2025—2028, Hdwb. d. Märchens II 178b.
Z33.p: A cumulative chain tale in which a series of characters eat or swallow one another or an object, in a single scene.

Z33.1.r: (First ed. Z31.3.1.) *Taylor JAFL XLVI 82 No. 2025; *Dh III 272; Fb “pandekage” II 782b; Danish: Kristensen Danske Dyrefabler 58f. Nos. 113—18; Norwegian: Christensen Norske Eventyr 149; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2025; Russian: Andrejev Nos. 295, 296*.
Z33.1.p: A woman makes a pancake that runs away, and various animals try in vain to stop it until a fox eats it.

Z33.2.r: When the mistress returns she says, “How fat you are!” The cat: “I ate the porridge, the bowl, and the ladle, and I will eat you.” The cat meets other animals and eats them after the same conversation. Finally eats too many. (First ed. Z31.3.2.) *Taylor JAFL XLVI 83 No. 2027; *Fb “kat” IV 255b; Danish: Kristensen Danske Dyrefabler 59ff. Nos. 119—130.
Z33.2.p: While the mistress is away, a cat eats the porridge, then the bowl, then the ladle.

Z33.3.r: “Good morning.” “Why are you up so early?” “I am not up so early. I have drunk seven vats of milk and eaten seven plates of porridge and I shall eat you.” She ate the pig. (First ed. Z31.3.3.) *Taylor JAFL XLVI 83 No. 2027A; Swedish: Norlander “Barnvisor och barnrim” Svenska Landsmålen V No. 5 n. 265.
Z33.3.p: A woman meets a pig in this chain tale. The note-free headline gives only this scene.

Z33.4.r: The troll: “I ate the five horses, I ate the watcher, and I will eat you.” Does so. Likewise the wife, servant, daughter, son, and dog. The cat scratches the troll open and rescues all. (First ed. Z31.3.4.) *Taylor JAFL XLVI 83 No. 2028; *Fb “ulv” III 970b, “æde” III 1139b, “bjørn” IV 43b; Danish: Kristensen Dyrefabler 68ff. Nos. 131—144; Swedish: T. Norlind Svenska Allmogens Liv@2 (Stockholm, 1925) 613; Russian: Andrejev No. 333B*.
Z33.4.p: A troll, or in some versions a wolf, eats a watchman's five horses and then the watchman himself. The master goes to investigate.

Z33.4.1.p: A louse and a crow make a pact of friendship, but the louse eats the crow despite the crow's warning that a single peck would kill the louse. The louse then eats a loaf, a goat, a cow, a buffalo, five soldiers, a wedding procession, an elephant, and a tank of water, until a soldier cuts the louse in two with his sword and frees them all.

Z33.4.2.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 162*; Russian: Andrejev No. 162*.
Z33.4.2.p: A wolf sings so that an old man surrenders his cattle, his children and grandchildren, and finally his wife. The old woman goes into the wolf's service and later returns home bringing butter and other goods.

Z39.r: (First ed. Z31.4.) Taylor JAFL XLVI 84 No. 2029.
Z39.p: A category for cumulative chain tales in which the links involve other events, and the members of the chain are not related to one another.

Z39.1.r: (First ed. Z31.4.1.) *Taylor JAFL XLVI 81 No. 2015; *BP I 348 n. 1, II 100, 104; Fb “gjed” IV 178a; Swedish: T. Norlind Svenska Allmogens Liv@2 (Stockholm, 1925) 613.
Z39.1.p: A goat refuses to go home, and one animal after another tries and fails to persuade it. In the end a wolf, or a bee in some versions, bites the goat and drives it home.

Z39.1.1.r: Final formula: The devil goes to strangle the Jew, the Jew to kill the ox, the ox to drink the water, the water to quench the fire, the fire to burn the stone, the stone to blunt the axe, the axe to cut the rope, the rope to tie the hunter, the hunter to shoot the goat—the goat leaves the hazel bush, the wee goat leaves the hazel bush. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2030.
Z39.1.1.p: A goat refuses to leave a hazel bush, and the tale proceeds as a chain of other animals trying and failing to move it.

Z39.2.r: (First ed. Z31.4.2.) *Taylor JAFL XLVI 81 No. 2016, Hdwb. d. Märchens II 176a; Jacobs English Fairy Tales 57; Danish: Kristensen Danske Dyrefabler 122ff. Nos. 230—37; Russian: Andrejev No. 2015 I*.
Z39.2.p: A cumulative nonsense tale about a little woman who owns a little cow, with the list of things and characters repeated and added to.

Z39.3.r: (Endless.) (First ed. Z31.4.3.) (Cf. Z11.) *Taylor JAFL XLVI 81 No. 2017, Hdwb. d. Märchens II 190a; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2017.
Z39.3.p: A crow gets stuck on a tarred bridge, its beak and tail sticking alternately to the tar as it tries to free itself.

Z39.4.r: What have you in your beak?—A knife.—etc. (Tile, water, ox, firewood, old woman, friars, mass, shirt.) (First ed. Z31.4.4.) *Taylor JAFL XLVI 80 No. 2011, Hdwb. d. Märchens II 174a; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 154 No. 2018A*.
Z39.4.p: A repeated question-and-answer chain in which a goose is asked where it has been and answers that it was in the fields.

Z39.4.1.p: A chain in which a titmouse is asked what it is eating and answers that it is a large turnip, and the exchange is repeated with further additions.

Z39.4.2.r: The owner will scold you. — I’ll sit on a pine tree, etc. Cheremis: Sebeok-Nyerges.
Z39.4.2.p: A chain in which a sparrow is asked where it is going and answers that it is going to eat seed.

Z39.5.r: Final formula: hen strips off feathers, rubbish heap catches fire, oak falls to ground, hare drowns self, magpie twists leg, ox breaks horns, river flows blood, maid breaks pails, housewife scatters dough. Master locks up wife and maid, goes to seek people more foolish. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2022*; Russian: Andrejev No. 241 III*; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 1963*.
Z39.5.p: A hen lays an egg and a mouse breaks it. Everyone grieves over the mishap and behaves extraordinarily, until the master puts an end to it.

Z39.6.r: “Why did you cut off the bell?”—“Why did you lay the block here, etc.” Cheremis: Sebeok-Nyerges.
Z39.6.p: A mother ties a bell on her child, and a cat cuts the bell off.

Z39.7.r: All refuse. Panther comes and devours her. India: Thompson-Balys.
Z39.7.p: Sisters leave a girl stuck in a tree. She asks a monkey, an ape, a bear and a tiger to lower her down, or else to bite her.

Z39.8.p: A small grain measure runs away when her husband beats her, and a series of suitors follows.

Z39.9.p: A mouse acquires a series of things, each offered in exchange for something else, through a long chain of trades. A girl accidentally kills the mouse at the end.

Z40.p: A category of cumulative tales in which each link depends on the next, so that one action can only happen once a previous one has happened.

Z41.r: The final formula is: cow give milk for cat; cat kill rat; rat gnaw rope; rope hang butcher; butcher kill ox; ox drink water; water quench fire; fire burn stick; stick beat dog; dog bite pig; pig jump over stile. (Various introductions.) (First ed. Z41.1.) *Taylor JAFL XLVI 84 No. 2030; *BP II 104, 108; **Goebel Hdwb. d. Märchens s.v. “Birnli” I 256ff.; *Emeneau JAFL LVI 272; Clouston Tales I 289; Köhler-Bolte I 136; Parsons JAFL XXXIII 34; Montet RTP VI 102; *Fb “and” IV 12;—Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 155 Nos. 2030A, B, C, D; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries Volksverhalen I 364 No. 21; Africa (Benga): Nassau 200 No. 30, (Hottentot): Bleek 33 No. 17, (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 177 No. 35, (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 392 No. 17, (Thonga): Junod 223; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 286 No. 138.
Z41.p: An old woman's pig will not jump over a stile so she can go home. She asks for help in vain until a cow gives her milk, which sets off a chain of required exchanges.

Z41.1.r: Recovery chain (similar to Z41). *Wesselski Hessische Blätter f. Vksk. XXXII 25.
Z41.1.p: A woman's meat, or liver, is stolen by a bird.

Z41.2.r: *Wesselski Hessische Blätter f. Vksk. XXXII 33; India: Thompson-Balys.
Z41.2.p: A crow must wash its bill before it can eat with the other birds. Water will give it only after a stag gives horn, which needs milk from a cow, and so on along the chain.

Z41.3.p: A conflict between a fowl and a thistle. The wind obeys and breaks the chain.

Z41.4.r: *Taylor JAFL XLVI 86 No. 2034, Hdwb. d. Märchens II 185b; *Wesselski Hessische Blätter f. Vksk. XXXII 28; *Newell JAFL XVIII (1905) 34 n. 1; BP II 107—8; Basset Contes Berbères No. 45, Nouveaux Contes Berbères No. 168.—England, U.S.: *Baughman.
Z41.4.p: A cat bites off a mouse's tail and will return it only for milk. The mouse must get milk from a cow, hay from a farmer, meat from a butcher and bread from a baker, with a locksmith and a miner also appearing in the chain.

Z41.4.1.r: Series of helpers similar to Z41.4. *Taylor JAFL XLVI 86 No. 2034A; *Wesselski Hessische Blätter f. Vksk. XXXII 28; BP II 107—8.
Z41.4.1.p: A mouse bursts open while crossing a stream.

Z41.4.2.r: *Taylor JAFL XLVI 86 No. 2034B; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 156 No. 2030D.
Z41.4.2.p: A dog holds a string but will give it up only if given bread. The cupboard wants a key, the smith wants charcoal, and so the chain runs through several exchanges, ending with a dove's feather given to the clouds.

Z41.5.r: Type 2034C*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2009*; Africa (Tonga): Torrend Specimens of Bantu Folklore (New York, 1921) 169ff., (Ila): Smith and Dale II 392ff. No. 17, (Pende): Frobenius Atlantis XI 265 No. 4, (Bassari): ibid. 97ff. No. 12, (Ashanti): Rattray 268 No. 73.
Z41.5.p: A chain of borrowing and repaying in which each repayment leads to a worse (or better) bargain than the one before.

Z41.6.r: Final formula: cat eats mouse, mouse cuts plant creeper, creeper snares elephant, elephant drinks up sea, sea quenches fire, fire burns stick, stick beats snake, snake bites queen, queen speaks to king, king chides carpenter, carpenter cuts mill handle, and pea is extracted. Questions in rhyme. India: Thompson-Balys.
Z41.6.p: A bird's pea gets stuck in the socket of a mill-handle, and the bird goes from one character to another asking for help, each refusing until a chain of favors gets the thing unstuck.

Z41.6.1.r: Final formula: at last creeper took pity on birds, and elephant feared creeper, and ocean feared elephant, and fire feared ocean, and stick feared fire, and snake feared stick, and carpenter feared snake; and carpenter split post which gave up the grain to the birds, who went away. India: Thompson-Balys.
Z41.6.1.p: A grain of parched grain sticks in a post, and a parrot goes to a raja and others for help getting it free.

Z41.7.r: Final formula: the worms begin to gnaw the rods, the rods to beat the oxen, the oxen to drink the water, the water to quench the fire, the fire to burn the hunters, the hunters to shoot the wolves, the wolves to kill the goats, the goats to gnaw the wormwood, the wormwood to rock me — it rocked and rocked me to sleep. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2003*.
Z41.7.p: A small bird is refused help by a wormwood plant when it asks the plant to rock it, so the bird asks others to make the plant cooperate in a chain of requests.

Z41.7.1.p: A boy gets his shoe dirty and asks a haystack to wipe it clean, starting a chain of requests in which each character needs something from the next before it will help.

Z41.8.r: Final formula: That was just what the cat was waiting for—it sprang to devour the mouse, the mouse to tear the spider’s web, the spider to entangle the dog, the dog to eat the goat, the goat to gnaw the rushes, the rushes to grow in the stream, the stream to quench the fire, the fire to burn the stone, the stone to beat the axe, the axe soon pulled out the needle that was stuck in the seamstress’s hand. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2005*.
Z41.8.p: A seamstress's needle is stuck in her hand and someone must pull it out, starting a chain of requests in which each helper needs something from another before helping.

Z41.9.r: “Lentils, lentils, get into my sack!” Final formula: the hungry hawk attacks the hens, the hens the worms, the worms the stick, the stick the ox, the ox runs to the water, the water attacks the fire, the fire the hunters, the hunters the wolf, the wolf the goat, the goat the willow, the willow the cat, the cat the mice, the mice the lentils, the lentils go whoosh whoosh into the sack. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2011*.
Z41.9.p: A lazy servant is involved with a grain of grain in a chain of events that shows his laziness.

Z42.r: The frost-bitten foot. Mouse perforates wall, wall resists wind, wind dissolves cloud, cloud covers sun, sun thaws frost, frost breaks foot. *Taylor JAFL XLVI 84 No. 2031, Hdwb. d. Märchens II 182ff.; **DeCock Volkssage 22—36; BP I 148 n. 2; Haavio FFC LXXXVIII 20; Köhler-Bolte II 47; Stiefel Zs. f. Vksk. V 448—50; Benfey Panchatantra I 373—78, II 264; Chauvin II 97f.; DeVries Volksverhalen I 1—3 No. 1, 356; Voorhoeve 166 No. 176; Clouston Tales I 309.—India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 384, (Zanzibar): Bateman 67 No. 5.
Z42.p: A cumulative tale in which each character is said to be stronger than the last, ending with the strongest one.

Z42.1.r: *Taylor JAFL XLVI 85 No. 2031A, Hdwb. d. Märchens II 184b; DeCock Volkssage 35f.; Oesterley No. 258; Köhler-Bolte II 55. —Jewish: Neuman.
Z42.1.p: A chain tale in which the strongest things are named in turn: wine, king, woman, and finally truth.

Z42.2.r: *Taylor JAFL XLVI 85 No. 2031B; Hdwb. d. Märchens II 184b; Köhler-Bolte I 578; Koran Surah 6, 75—78; *Basset RTP VII 397; Jewish: Neuman.
Z42.2.p: Abraham, at nightfall, worships a star, then the moon, then the sun, and finally gives up idol worship to worship God.

Z42.3.p: A Brahmin worships an idol and makes daily offerings to it; when a rat eats the offerings he worships the rat, then a cat that eats the rat, then his wife, and finally himself as most powerful.

Z43.r: The final formula is: Fountain give up water for forest, forest give up wood for baker, baker give up bread for dog, dog give up hairs to cure the cock. (Variant: mouse loses tail.) *Taylor JAFL XLVI 85 No. 2032; *BP II 107; Norlind Svenska Allmogens Liv@2 (Stockholm, 1925) 613 “Tupen och hänen”; Haavio FFC LXXXVIII 89 n. 1; RTP XV 220.—Russian: Andrejev No. 241 I; N. A. Indian (Zuñi): Cushing 411.
Z43.p: A mouse drops a nut that hits a cock on the head and steals the cock's whiskers, so the cock goes to an old woman to be cured.

Z43.1.r: *Wesselski Hessische Blätter f. Vksk XXXII 24; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 156 No. 2032A*.
Z43.1.p: A toad asks a magpie to throw down a chestnut; the magpie breaks its beak, and the toad must go through a chain of requests for a horsehair to tie it up again.

Z43.2.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2030G; Livonian: Looritz FFC LXVI No. 241@1; Russian: Andrejev No. 241 II*.
Z43.2.p: A cock blames a hazel bush for tearing its clothes, and each character blames the next in a chain of accusations ending with the wolf.

Z43.3.p: A nut hits a cock on the head and he thinks the world is coming to an end, so he sends word along a chain of animals to warn each other.

Z43.4.p: A fly frightens a snake, the snake frightens rats, the rats frighten a monkey, and so on through a chain of creatures each scaring the next.

Z44.1.p: An old man is supposed to build a house for a woman, who has some beans for him, but a goat eats the beans.

Z45.r: (First ed. Z41.9.) *Taylor JAFL XLVI 87 No. 2039; *BP III 335—37.
Z45.p: A cumulative chain of cause and effect in which a lost horseshoe nail leads step by step to a lost shoe, horse, and rider, the whole disaster blamed on that one small nail.

Z46.p: A cumulative tale whose events build to an extreme climax of misfortunes, where the magpie is dead.

Z47.p: A series of tricks in which each item is traded away for the next, forming a chain of exchanges.

Z47.1.p: A tricky fox sings a formula of exchanges as he swaps a razor for a pot, the pot for a bride, and the bride for a drum.

Z49.p: A miscellaneous category of tales built on chains of interdependent events, where each item causes or depends on the next.

Z49.1.r: Z41.7.) *Taylor JAFL XLVI 87 No. 2037; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 155 No. 2026*.
Z49.1.p: A cumulative chain of killings: a man kills his grandmother for refusing to cook a hare, then kills a priest who judged his crime, and a friar absolves him to save himself from being killed.

Z49.2.r: Boys get help. One of them injures the helper. Pursued. Hidden by kind hen. One injures the hen. Hen pursues, etc. (First ed. Z41.8.) *Taylor JAFL XLVI 87 No. 2038; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 264f. No. 70.
Z49.2.p: A cumulative chase in which each creature in turn is pursued or refuses to help, so the chain of pursuit grows longer.

Z49.2.1.r: Final formula: the scythe cuts the creeper loose. India: Thompson-Balys.
Z49.2.1.p: A cumulative pursuit in which a fat mouse cannot get into its hole, and it asks a carpenter to shave flesh off its ribs, but he refuses.

Z49.3.p: A man punishes a mango-bird for eating mangoes by beating and mistreating it in turn, but the bird shows no pain, and at last it flies out of the man's nose so that he dies.

Z49.4.r: At last: “Shall I tell it again?” (First ed. Z41.12.) *Taylor JAFL XLVI 81 No. 2013.
Z49.4.p: A cumulative rhyme in which each new person is introduced as the child or relative of the previous one, growing a long chain of family members.

Z49.5.r: Where is the fire?—The water quenched it. (First ed. Z41.13.) Type 2018.
Z49.5.p: A question-and-answer chain in which a lost or burned store is blamed on one cause after another, each answer causing the next.

Z49.5.1.r: “Where is that cock?”—“He drowned in the sea.”—“Where is that sea?”—“It is grown over with reeds.”—“Where are those reeds?”—“The maids have cut them down”, etc. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2018.
Z49.5.1.p: Someone asks where some grain is and is told a cock snatched it, forming a short chain of blame.

Z49.5.2.r: He keeps on asking: “Shall I then be able to eat?” Decides he will not have enough patience to make bread. (Cf. K555.1.2.) Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 164*.
Z49.5.2.p: A wolf wants to make bread, and a farmer explains to him how bread is made, the wolf trying to follow the steps.

Z49.6.p: A trial held among the animals in which the matter of blame passes through a chain of creatures and accidents.

Z49.6.1.p: Birds fight and their fighting causes a series of accidents that harm other animals and people.

Z49.6.2.p: A bite or prick sets off a series of accidents, each creature harming the next.

Z49.6.3.p: A cumulative chain tale in which a man cutting bamboo sets off a sequence: a falling fruit hits a bird, the bird scratches an ant's nest, the ant bites a boar, and the chain continues until an old woman falls into a well.

Z49.7.p: A cumulative tale in which a bird seeks a carpenter to free its young trapped in a closed tree, and a beetle's bite starts a chain of events that eventually frees them: beetle bites calf, calf bites cow, cow hoofs carpenter, carpenter beats wife, hunters save his cow, and the carpenter releases the birds.

Z49.8.r: Final formula: Forester attacks bear, the bear the wolf, the wolf the dog, the dog the cat, the cat the mouse, the mouse the grain—the grain is bitten in two. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2006*.
Z49.8.p: A tale in which someone bites a grain in half, forming a small link in a chain of events.

Z49.9.r: Final formula: The mouse holds onto the cat, the cat holds onto Mary, Mary holds onto Annie, Annie holds onto grandmother, grandmother holds onto grandfather, grandfather holds onto the turnip—they all pull and pull it out. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2008*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1960G*.
Z49.9.p: A cumulative tale of people pulling one another in a chain to uproot a turnip, each joining the pull in turn.

Z49.10.p: A chain of animals eating one another: a lizard eats a cricket, a frog eats the lizard, a snake eats the frog, and an eagle eats the snake, until a man shoots the eagle and takes it home, so only the lizard escapes.

Z49.11.r: (One person blames another who blames another, etc.) India: *Thompson-Balys.
Z49.11.p: A question about who is to blame for an accident, where responsibility passes along a chain of causes.

Z49.11.1.r: (The chain: mason—cement mixer—beautifully singing woman—pearl necklace—jeweller—diver—sea.) India: *Thompson-Balys.
Z49.11.1.p: A wall under construction falls down, and after a long chain of blame the king finally learns that the sea is the one responsible.

Z49.11.2.p: A thief breaks his leg climbing a wall to rob a house, and he sues the owner for having a dangerous wall.

Z49.12.p: A hermit must obtain a cat to kill rats, but the cat needs milk from a cow, and so on through a chain of linked requests and favors that each depend on the next.

Z49.13.p: A chain of killings: a bulbul destroys a flower and is killed by a cat, the cat is shaken by a dog, the dog is killed by a boy, and the king sentences the boy to death.

Z49.14.p: A cumulative tale in which an old woman swallows a fly, then a spider to catch the fly, then a bird, a dog, a cow, and finally a horse, each to catch the one before.

Z51.p: A cumulative tale whose chain is built on contradictions or extremes, where the story piles up opposite or exaggerated events.

Z51.1.p: A chain of events in which a house is burned down, as the story piles up its misfortunes.

Z52.p: A bird takes revenge for its caged mate: it builds a cart, yokes frogs to it, arms itself with a piece of reed, and declares war on the king.
